Our proposed method introduces a new feature extraction technique that surpasses
content-based filtering using all item attributes simultaneously, not just the top-ranked
features. To test this approach, we created a dataset comprising 50,000 movies rated
by 2,000 users, and employed Python's Keras library to build and evaluate our model.
The results reveal a 25% enhancement in performance over the baseline method, and
all conducted experiments yield a p-value less than 0.05, indicating our findings
are statistically significant.

Complex, multi-conditional systems pose significant analytical challenges, largely because the fundamental principle of independence of conditions does not apply. As a result, the basic concepts of entropy and mutual information need to be re-expressed to accommodate these complexities, as demonstrated by prior works. In contrast, this paper showcases the effectiveness of a novel approach that reframes these conditional systems as a special type of graphical models, where the conditions become part of the graph structure. By doing so, the paper derives closed-form expressions for the information-theoretic metrics, as well as their extremal values, for the specific case of XOR networks - a family of highly complex, multi-conditional functions. The paper further investigates the intriguing phenomenon that the extremal values of the conditional entropy and mutual information can be positive, setting a new baseline for future studies of these networks. The research on these networks also raises important implications for the study of computational complexity and the interplay between randomness and computation.

This paper focuses on resolving polysemy in English by proposing a novel
approach that leverages BERT-based models and a custom-built dataset. We
initially examined multiple BERT-based sentence representations and
classification models before selecting a methodological combination that
yielded the best results. We used a BERT-based sentence similarity model,
GlossBERT, in conjunction with BERT-based classification models to
disambiguate word senses. Furthermore, we presented a newly constructed
dataset called Senti4S-Eng, a set of sentiment analysis tasks designed
for sentence sense disambiguation. Our results indicated that
classifying sentences based on the same base sense produced an average
f1-score of 79.35 when using Huang et al.'s. GlossBERT approach.

Reasoning about procedures from various sources of expertise, particularly those presented through different modalities, is an important aspect of human comprehension. While humans naturally understand complex workflows from different sources, such as video instructions and text recipes, AI systems have significant difficulty in this area. Our research addresses this challenge by developing a data set that includes complementary presentations of expertise in different modalities and tests the ability of AI systems to provide step-by-step instructions for achieving a goal. We discovered that existing models are not capable of understanding complex procedures from various sources of expertise by a significant margin. We also found some models to be highly skilled at understanding individual presentations of expertise, but these models struggled to integrate this understanding when faced with presentations of expertise in different modalities. We were able to improve the performance of the models on this task by a significant margin through the use of cross-modal attention and the incorporation of semantic meaning, but they still had a long way to go in terms of accurately understanding complex procedures from various sources of expertise.

In the study of random graphs, a few key concepts have been widely exploited, including the giant component, the survival probability, and the cavity distribution. Though individually important, these concepts have not been comprehensively integrated into a unified framework within the context of random regular graphs. This dissertation aims to expand on this foundation by applying graph-theoretic tools to cavity distribution theory, thereby gaining insight into epidemic and percolation phenomena on Cayley graphs. A novel expression for the cavity probability is derived for $k$-ary trees, demonstrating that the number of leaves scales as $k^{1.5}\text{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ in random regular graphs. By further establishing the relationship between the local structure and the cavity distribution, it is demonstrated that the number of leaves in $k$-ary trees follows a binomial distribution. This localized approach is then used to model the behavior of the spread of an infection on random regular graphs, obtaining closed-form expressions for the final number of infected nodes and the impact of varying transmission probabilities. This generalized framework is also applied to the specific case of graph propagation on $k$-ary trees.

A fundamental property of the standard Airy polynomial $A_n(x)$ is its universality, which is reflected in the fact that as $n$ approaches infinity, the normalized polynomial $\frac{A_n(\sqrt{n}x+n^{1/6}u)}{\sqrt{n}}$ converges to a deterministic function for almost every $u$ in the real numbers. This note confirms that the standard Airy polynomial $A_n(x)$ achieves the optimal bulk universality result for a broad class of polynomials $p_n(x)$ whose zeros exhibit the same asymptotic behavior as those of $A_n(x)$. In addition, it establishes that the edge universality of $A_n(x)$ also holds under the same conditions.

Our research involves creating advanced gravitational wave detectors that utilize a unique sensor design called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer to improve their response to high-frequency signals. By leveraging a novel method of laser reflection off a slowly moving mass within an enclosure, these detectors can discern millisecond gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers and other events. To validate their effectiveness, we employed numerical simulations to model the response of these sensors to gravitational waves in various scenarios, including the binary neutron star mergers detected by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and the Advanced LIGO detectors. The results showed that the sloshing Sagnac interferometers' response can be improved by optimizing their design parameters, particularly their enclosure size. Furthermore, we observed that the response of the sloshing Sagnac interferometers can be distinguished from that of conventional Sagnac interferometers using their energy spectrum.

A new MIMO protocol, called XL-MIMO, has been proposed and it claims to significantly increase the number of active devices that can be accommodated in a cellular network, primarily by taking into consideration the spatial characteristics of complex wireless channels. Researchers have analyzed the visibility areas of various devices within this protocol and demonstrated that, assuming certain conditions are met, their visibility areas will not intersect with each other. Based on this non-intersection property, they develop an analytical model that can predict the protocol's performance and identify optimal scheduling options for a large number of active devices. Simulations confirm that the XL-MIMO protocol can support a substantially higher number of active devices, up to 100 times more, than traditional MIMO protocols, without a significant decrease in spectral efficiency.

Recent observations of young stellar objects using mid infrared cameras have significantly improved, and can now detect the structures within their surrounding protoplanetary disks. A previous study discovered various spatial patterns in disks surrounding young objects, and suggested they could be the early signs of planet formation. In this study, we utilize a sophisticated computer model to simulate the effects of these structures on the temperature and motion of the material in the disks. We then analyze the visibility of these patterns when observed from different angles, and as the disks rotate, to predict what they would appear like in mid infrared images. Our results show that in some cases, the patterns may only be visible for a short period during their orbital movement around the star, and that the orientation of the disks can make some patterns harder to see. We also found that the motion of the material in the disks can make some patterns appear as if they are moving. These findings suggest that by studying the patterns in mid infrared images of the disks surrounding young objects, we can learn more about the early stages of planet formation.

The term "Big Apple strength" is used to describe nucleon combinations that exceed 50 MeV of energy and far exceed the expected energy of typical nuclear matter. Researchers have discovered that the strong interaction among nucleons contributes significantly to the abundance of "Big Apple strengths". They also found that the vast majority of these "Big Apple strengths" have very low probabilities of being observed in scattering experiments. Only a small fraction can be detected because of their unique "symmetry" properties. It is proposed that the extensive presence of "Big Apple strengths" contributes to the stability of finite nuclei and might also be responsible for certain astronomical phenomena such as the magnetic fields found in white dwarfs, neutron stars, and even the sun.

Using a first-principles DMFT approach on the real-frequency line, we have investigated the electronic properties of SrMnO$_3$ to better understand the results obtained from a simplified model used to study the metal-insulator transition in this material. In this calculation, we used a large cubic cell to account for the strong correlation between electrons localized in the $3d$ orbitals of the manganese atoms. We performed an extra step to remove the artificial effects caused by the interaction between electrons in adjacent cells, and found that this is crucial for obtaining accurate results. We used a parametrized model that includes the hybridization between $d$ orbitals in different cells, and found that this has a significant impact on the spectral function, especially when the energy difference between two particular levels, $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$, is large. We used this approach to measure the density of states in SrMnO$_3$, and found that it is in good agreement with the results obtained from an extra-ordinary process experiment. Additionally, we used this approach to study the L-edge absorption spectrum of SrMnO$_3$, and found that it is in good agreement with the results obtained from an XMCD experiment.

This research focuses on developing resilient M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates capable of withstanding frequency errors that affect multiple motional modes in trapped ions. By incorporating a broad-spectrum application of Doppler shifts, we incorporate all motional modes equally, linking their peak amplitudes and enabling the implementation of uniform rotations between any number of modes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using a range of trapped ion systems from two to ten $^{168}$Yb$^+$ ions and show that it can robustly perform MS gates with low errors even when subject to significant frequency deviations, specifically when dealing with larger numbers of motional modes.

The unique properties of gigahertz-range dielectric resonances in paraelectric phases are difficult to understand without considering the local structure. However, the existing models are typically based on macroscopic concepts, without connection to the actual atomic arrangement. To bridge this gap, we used advanced neutron scattering and X-ray diffraction techniques to create a detailed description of the local structure in barium titanate at its Curie temperature. By analyzing this data, we developed a comprehensive picture of how Titanval atoms are arranged, including how they deviate from a perfect lattice and how this affects the local electric field. This advanced understanding of the local structure enabled us to explain the unique features of the dielectric resonances in this material, and it has implications for other perovskite materials as well.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on combining 2D materials, like graphene and TMDCs, to create van der Waal heterostructures that combine the exceptional properties of these individual components. By incorporating a patterned electrical potential, it is now feasible to produce artificial materials consisting of connected quantum wells that mimic the behavior of Dirac metals. However, the electronic properties of these artificial metals depend on the orientation of the Dirac cones within the combined system. In order to overcome this constraint, researchers have proposed using a rotationally asymmetric potential design to link the Dirac cones in three directions. However, this approach faces a major challenge when implemented in TMDC-based systems due to the large size of the atomic lattice. Consequently, implementing a $\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}$ superlattice to modulate the electronic properties via the Froehlich mechanism appears more viable. This approach modulates the energy levels of the combined system's atomic orbitals, effectively bridging the energy gap and linking the Dirac cones in three directions. By applying a uniform magnetic field, researchers have observed the opening of gaps in the quasi-flat bands along the Fermi surfaces along the X points in the Brillouin zone, resulting in zero-field conduction localized near the edge of the superlattice. In contrast, the quasi-flat band's non-zero energy distinguishes it from the zero-energy flat band phenomenon. Furthermore, the quasi-flat band shows unique characteristics, such as non-trivial

We introduce a general framework that encompasses bimodal frequency ratios, which involve the number of times an event of one type occurs between two separate events of a different type occurring. This framework expands upon a previous concept called the gap arrangement, which was initially proposed by Hunter and Auerbach, and was used to analyze bimodal frequency ratios. Our proposed framework is a more comprehensive framework that allows for various combinations of arranged events, and as a result, it yields a more extensive range of possible bimodal frequency ratios.

We have calculated the branching ratio for the decay $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ where $N$ represents either a neutron or a proton. By combining various contributions to this decay, we find the dominant process to be the neutral current one, with an estimated branching ratio of around $4.507 \times 10^{-10}$. This can be compared to the expected sensitivity of the NA62 experiment, which could reach a limit of $1.9 \times 10^{-10}$ with a certain configuration. Additionally, we determined the most influential variables that affect the branching ratio and the NA62 experiment's sensitivity, which can be significant in interpreting NA62's future findings.

In a Sagnac interferometer, typically used for detecting gyrosopic effects, we find unusual spectral anomalies in both linear and circular configurations when considering the Galilean frame. Typically, a linearly polarized light source experiences no change in polarization after passing through the interferometer in any frame. However, when accounting for relativistic effects, a tiny shift in polarization angle becomes apparent, primarily caused by the longitudinal component of the light's momentum vector. This anomaly, however, displays an unanticipated disparity when examining the circular Sagnac interferometer, resulting in a spectral anomaly that cannot be explained by classical electrodynamics. A detailed derivation is provided for the spectral anomaly in both linear and circular configurations, revealing that the latter's anomaly is equivalent to approximately twice the shift experienced by the linear configuration.

This work extends the research of Fittouhi and Kraemer on parabolic adjoint connections, Weierstrass segments, and nilpotent elements for Lie algebras of type $A$. It introduces the concept of a Weierstrass segment for a long root $\alpha$ as a set $\Delta_\alpha$ containing $\alpha$ and defined by the equation $\Delta_\alpha = \{\delta \in \Phi_{\text{re}} \mid \beta + \delta \in \Phi_{\text{re}}\}$, demonstrating that it is a union of roots and the highest weight of the irreducible highest weight module $L_\Delta$ is $2\rho_{\text{re}}$ when $\Delta$ is a Weierstrass segment. Furthermore, when $\Delta$ is a single root $\alpha$, the highest weight module $L_\Delta$ is isomorphic to the irreducible highest weight module $L_{1+\alpha}$ for a positive root $\alpha$. It also proves that the parabolic adjoint operation with respect to a root $\alpha$ corresponds to the derived functors of the local cohomology functors $\mathbb{H}^i_\alpha$ for a classical affine Lie algebra. Neural language models have historically required massive amounts of
training data, which can be costly to produce. High-quality training data
typically involves human-generated content, but its creation is also expensive
and time-consuming. As an alternative to starting from scratch, existing
methods typically attempt to expand existing corpora using seed texts or
seed words. Although successful in certain applications, such approaches have
limitations when it comes to generating nuanced, real-language training datasets
for neural models. For example, the next word prediction task in language modeling
can be quite complex, involving more than just the n-1 preceding words. In this
research, we propose a novel way to incorporate n-gram structures into neural
models, allowing them to learn from existing multi-word patterns within existing
corpora. We further suggest the use of a residual learning model that can
effectively learn from both a general n-gram linguistic model and a model specific
to a particular domain. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on three
different datasets and find that it outperforms both the n-gram model and a
transformer-based baseline model.

We've derived three $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano trifold threefolds w.r.t. Giventhal's construction, leading to a $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano trifold by combining two $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano surfaces using a type of transformation called the Laurent transformation.

Reconstructing and identifying individuals from their facial images is a complex task due to the high degree of variability in human faces resulting from different factors such as lighting conditions, image quality, and attempts to conceal one's identity. To address this issue, a robust 3D face reconstruction method is needed that can handle imperfect two-dimensional facial data and guard against manipulation of the input images. Toward this goal, we introduce a pioneering approach that utilizes a pair of pre-trained convolutional neural networks to analyze two facial images simultaneously and align a set of facial points across the two images. To enhance this approach, we implemented several techniques including mutual correction, cross-checking, and bound constraints on the positions of the points. To handle image degradation and attempts at disguise, we integrated a degraded facial super-resolution module into our model. Extensive experiments demonstrated the superiority of our method over alternative approaches, including a comparison with a leading method that only handled undistorted faces, showing a notable improvement of 8.85% in accuracy. Additionally, our method outperformed other 3D face reconstruction approaches in benchmark tests, including a comparison with a method that only handled ideal 2D data, resulting in a 12.75% improvement in accuracy.

We investigate two separate systems where the translation symmetry is broken, by comparing their corresponding effective descriptions in terms of field theories. Our study specifically focuses on two discrete, spatial periodic systems: a one-dimensional lattice containing dopant atoms and a two-dimensional bragg mirror cavity. We demonstrate that the dopant lattice's effective theory exhibits fractonic behavior, whereas the bragg mirror cavity's model does not. Ultimately, we seek to understand why these two systems yield distinct effective theories, and how this difference relates to the boundary between stable and unstable modes in periodic systems that experience translation symmetry breakdown.

Inflationary cosmology leads to the generation of perturbations in the early universe, which can result in the formation of black holes of a certain mass range if certain conditions are met in a specific $\alpha$-attractor inflation model. If an in-depth examination of certain fluctuations during inflation can yield sufficient amplification of perturbations, then it could be possible for black holes to form as a result of these perturbations in a specific $\alpha$-attractor inflation model. It has been found that in a particular $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, an examination of certain fluctuations during inflation can yield perturbations of a certain type, with amplitudes that are in line with a set of constraints placed upon them by the principles of $\alpha$-attractor inflation. However, in a specific $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, an examination of certain fluctuations during inflation can only result in perturbations being amplified by a certain amount, which is not sufficient to meet the requirements necessary for the formation of black holes of a certain mass range. Nevertheless, it has been discovered that in a particular $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, an examination of certain fluctuations during inflation can yield perturbations of a certain type, with amplitudes that are in line with a set of constraints placed upon them by the principles of $\alpha$-attractor inflation, and that these perturbations can be of a certain type that could potentially result in the formation

An ordered tree is labeled if its edges are assigned a linear order. A key aspect of this structure is the concept of a deepest vertex, which refers to a node with the lowest elevation. Due to the absence of a parental relationship in ordered trees, the term 'child' is actually a misnomer for certain nodes with the lowest elevation. In this study, we seek to identify the number of deepest vertices in an ordered tree, denoted as the multiset $\mathcal{M}_T$ for a given labeled tree $T$. In our initial exploration, we examine the number of deepest vertices in binary trees, catering to the case where the elevation difference between certain nodes is zero. Our formal proof involves the use of a recursive approach, supported by explicit equations for certain levels of trees. In contrast, we approach the more general case of n-ary trees through induction, with a focus on the relationship between a tree and its children.

Our district-specific OCR system uses a rule-based approach to correct optical character recognition errors, ensuring accuracy in ballot count translations. Despite advancements in OCR technology, certain issues such as font variations, misalignment, and overlapping text continue to impede its effectiveness in translating ballot counts. In high-stakes election audits, completely reliable OCR software is crucial, but the only method to achieve 100% accuracy is through human review of all ballot images and resulting translations. Our team designed an election-specific OCR system to validate the use of optical character recognition in translating ballot counts, as there are no established methods for evaluating OCR software against real-world election data. Our research includes a district-specific test case, but to maintain neutrality, the specific election data used cannot be disclosed. Nonetheless, our study demonstrates that a rule-based approach can boost the accuracy of OCR translations to above 99.9%, and it is feasible to implement an election-specific OCR system with minimal technical expertise required. As a result, we are making our system's code available for public use, in the hope that it will contribute positively to the continuation of transparent and accessible election processes.

Moreover, we find that under the condition $X^T\Sigma X = \frac{n}{h}\lambda^2 I_d$, which measures the stiffness of $X$, a critical threshold $\kappa^*$ exists for the matrix $X$ such that:

Speech enhancement, whether for primary or auxiliary systems like speech recognition and subband processing, is highly dependent on signal quality. A crucial factor in these systems' performance is the quality of the input speech. For instance, poor speech quality can lead to misclassification in speech recognition. Furthermore, noisy speech can result in lower system reliability in various applications like video conferencing. Therefore, it is essential to investigate methods that can enhance the quality of speech under noisy conditions. Certain deep learning-based speech enhancement frameworks have been successful in processing white Gaussian noise; however, they tend to perform inadequately when confronted with non-stationary and intermittent types of noise commonly encountered in real-world environments. Moreover, the majority of these frameworks overlook the possibility of noise present in training data affecting the performance of their subsequent speech recognition systems. To address these challenges, a novel bidirectional deep learning attention model has been proposed that leverages training data with inherent background noise. The proposed model's architecture is a bidirectional attention-based deep learning framework that incorporates multiple layers, where each layer builds on the previous one while being uniquely optimized to tackle distinct frequency ranges. Notably, the use of background noise during training enables the model to focus on distinguishing between the speech and background noise, resulting in enhanced performance when tested with various types of noise. The proposed framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a range of noisy conditions during training and testing. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of objective quality

Information diffusion through recommendation systems can have sinister underpinnings, as we demonstrate by hazardous means. We've developed a novel technique for infiltrating these systems by creating infectious "songs" that spread music recommendations containing a deadly payload. We've successfully tested this method on multiple platforms, exploiting human psychology to spread our "viral" content. We've also examined potential countermeasures and found them to be inadequate, highlighting the urgency of developing more effective safeguards against such attacks.

As decentralized, stateless, and stateful storage systems continue to grow in the industry, understanding autonomous storage provisioning strategies becomes increasingly important. We have developed a mathematical framework for modeling storage demand and supply in a decentralized market, and leveraged this to test various self-scheduling strategies for a swarm of storage components within a data center. Our results show that centrally optimized policies perform best, but that gradient-based methods can also yield favorable outcomes in a decentralized environment, especially when combined with cautious learning policies that account for the risks of misclassification. When applied to a real-world dataset, these strategies indicate that a 24% increase in storage coexistence can be achieved with only a 10% increase in conflict risk.

In matter, the absorption of x-rays is typically dominated by two processes: scattering and absorption that leads to changes within the target, such as the release of electrons during Auger-Meitner decay. However, a new phenomenon occurs when using x-ray pulses with sufficient intensity and a specific duration, where the time-dependent phase of the x-ray field causes a shift in the phase of the emitted electron wave train. This effect becomes most pronounced in cases with a high initial state density, such as in the (K) state of atoms, and results in the appearance of an interference pattern in the electron yield detected over time. This phenomenon is referred to as x-ray interelectrode effect and is a manifestation of the phase space interference that occurs when two coherent electron wave trains are generated by the interaction of a strong x-ray field with a target that has a high initial state density. The occurrence of this effect was confirmed through an experimental and theoretical analysis of K-edge absorption at a hydrogen-like neon target using 40 fs x-ray pulses, and the results showed best match with a parameter-free theoretical model when the same data and theoretical calculations were compared. The validity of this phenomenon has been further confirmed by observing the same interference pattern when using two x-ray pulses with opposing phases, and this observation is in line with a 100% visibility of the interference pattern. The occurrence of this effect could potentially be used in the development of sensitive detectors that can identify the duration of x-ray pulses.

We examined how different planetary systems influence atmospheric circulation in gas giants, comparing the outcomes from two simplified global circulation models representing planets with rapid rotation rates. MR94 mimics the circulation of highly inclined winds found in rapidly rotating planets through cyclostrophic forces, while MR91 is sensitive to geostrophic forces and can produce band-like wind patterns. By analyzing the MR94 model with various Nondimensional Rotation Rates and comparing its outcomes to the MR91 model, we explored how rescaled parameters affect atmospheric circulation. When the rotation rate is low enough to ignore cyclostrophic forces, the MR94 model is similar to the MR91 model, producing wind patterns similar to those in Jupiter and Saturn. However, as the rotation rate accelerates, the MR94 model shifts towards wind patterns characteristic of super-rotating equatorial jets and counter-rotating jet streams. The MR94 model's wind patterns change significantly as the rotation rate increases, but the MR91 model remains relatively stable. Due to its rapid circulation and band-like wind patterns, MR94 is likened to an idealized turbostrophic turbulence model. The distinct outcomes of these models highlight the diversity of atmospheric circulation patterns driven by rotation rates in various exotic worlds, as inferred from their magnetic field observations, and suggest that future missions should prioritize magnetic field data to better understand the circulation behind these field patterns in planets and moons like Jupiter's moon Ganymede.

In our investigation, we discovered that learning in deep neural networks is significantly
more efficient when data is presented in an ordered manner based on image intensity.
Our hypothesis suggests that ordered presentation facilitates effective exploitation of
nonlinear signal processing elements in multiple network layers.
To test this hypothesis, we utilized a simple circuit simulation and found that
ordered presentation helps to minimize signal distortion.
To further improve learning efficiency, we proposed two innovative techniques:
first, a method to identify optimal intensity ranges for each layer and second, a
technique to adjust network architecture during training based on signal processing
capabilities.
The results of our experiments showed that these techniques lead to a notable
improvement in training time, and when combined with batch normalization,
further optimize performance.

This study discloses novel aspects of the algebraic frequency domain of a 5G non-orthogonal multiple-access (NOMA) system. Initially, we derive compact mathematical expressions that capture important characteristics of 5G-NOMA "difference" and "sum" functions. Subsequently, we interpret these expressions through a geometric perspective, utilizing tools from complex geometry. Notably, our analytical framework is applicable to a broader class of multi-NOMA systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the minimum distance between distinct algebraic frequency domain points of a multi-NOMA system directly impacts its security, with implications for future frequency-domain communications.

We suggest creating a novel source of correlated photons using dipolar species in optical resonators. Our proposal leverages the long-lived nature of these particles to delay optical assessments, enabling the rapid production of paired photons in a squeezed state. By manipulating the dipolar interaction in a tripartite system - comprising a photon cavity and a target species - we achieve this source of correlated photons. Notably, this system can be used to enhance optical measurements on the target species by applying the Chiribella et al. strategy, potentially raising its state fidelity following interaction.

By utilizing the effective weight theory, which segregates valley and crystallographic variations, our model simulates donor electron behavior in silicon using the complete configuration interaction method. Our approach uses a general donor electron potential function, incorporating exchange and direct terms, to calculate effective weights at different valley and orbital levels. We accurately accounted for valley and orbital mixing by applying the Kane model and relevant energy differences. We obtained a comprehensive donor electron profile, exchange-linked behavior, and direct and exchange interaction effects on valley and orbital levels. The results show that in silicon, donor electrons exhibit unique configurations, with exchange interaction causing mixing between different valley and orbital levels. The weights of these configurations depend on the donor's configuration and location within the lattice. We simulated the electronic behavior of silicon phosphorus double donors, confirming previous findings of exchange-linked $V_{0}$ and $X^{0}_{A-X}$ states. The weight of the valley-orbital superposition increases with the donor-electron number and decreases with the confining potential. We also found that in silicon/germanium superlattices, the weight of the orbital level can be adjusted over a range of 0.1-0.9 by varying the silicon layer thickness from one monolayer to four.

Our investigation reveals that not only do HgTe quantum trenches exhibit gapless behavior, but also when coupled with CdTe layers, the resulting structures display unique, Dirac-like points. We demonstrate that this phenomenon occurs when the width of the HgTe layer falls within a specific range, bridging the ordinary and extraordinary regions. We observe the evolution of these Dirac points by manipulating the HgTe layer width, achieving this by utilizing lateral electrical gating. We measure the conductance along the edges of these quantum trenches to gain insight into their transport properties. When the Fermi level is positioned at the Dirac points, we quantify the conductance to be $\sigma_0=2e^2/h$. Furthermore, we manipulate the potential to move the Fermac to the valence and conduction bands, inducing skew-scattering and snell-like refraction in the corresponding energy levels.

This research examines how a new adaptive protocol for Layered Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (LC-NOMA) performs under dynamic scenarios at road intersections. We particularly focus on investigating the effects of capacity, delay, and reliability on LC-NOMA's efficiency. An in-depth analysis of a simulation based on the MiXIM mobility dataset revealed that LC-NOMA's efficiency reaches 95.4% in terms of capacity, 91.5% for delay, and 95.2% for reliability at road intersections. Notably, LC-NOMA's performance is most sensitive to queue length, with implications for system design and future research on LC-NOMA.

A crucial aspect of Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD) is dealing with conflicts that arise when multiple applications require different allocation periods for communication. We propose a new, more flexible TDD model that considers these conflicts and can accommodate a variety of applications with varying communication schedules. We also develop a game-theoretic approach to analyzing this model's performance, and use a specific example to show its effectiveness. In this example, we can achieve a 25% increase in network throughput compared to a static TDD network.

This paper delves into the Hall anomaly within a fixed lattice of vortices in a thin Y-Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_{n+1}$Cu$_{n}$O$_{2n+1}$ $n$-layered thin films by comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions. According to our theoretical model, the Hall anomaly is composed of distinct irregular peaks at pinning sites and should be described by a long-range potential function, in contrast to previous models that are limited by local interactions within the vortex core. By integrating the quantity of charge $e$ with the velocity field at each pinning site, we are able to calculate the Hall anomaly IR spectrum, and our experimental results support the existence of this phenomenon for both strong and weak pinning cases, with the Hall anomaly IR spectrum displaying peak and step-like behavior respectively.

Using the exact dynamic renormalization group, we investigate the behavior of spin correlation decoupling coefficients in the three-dimensional Ising model near its critical point. These coefficients represent the linear combinations of magnetization cumulants that remain invariant under a rotation in the n-dimensional cumulant space. We find that in three dimensions, a specific subset of these coefficients exhibits the same critical behavior as the magnetization correlation length, with universal critical exponents that match those of the corresponding correlation function. Furthermore, we find that in the n=4 dimension, the fourth cumulant displays an universal infinite period of instability before settling into a fixed point, characteristic of a universal dynamical transition in higher dimensional systems.

A commuting square of hyperfinite subfactors with low index is used to create a sequence of subfactors. When combined with a square root of the original square, this process results in a family of subfactors on a type of Hilbert space. We refer to this process as 'decentralization.' A key aspect of this process is understood through the application of central sequence approximations. We have discovered that a specific, defined set of operators plays a crucial role in generating the subsequent subfactors in the sequence. We refer to this set as the 'decentralizing sequence.' We have also identified specific properties of this sequence, including its relationship to the square root of the original square, and its behavior at infinite depth. Notably, we have shown that the subfactors in the sequence have low index, and their central sequence approximations converge to a commuting square with properties similar to those of the original square.

In this work, we introduce a novel neural network model called the Gradient Hamiltonian Neural Network (GHNN) that acquires full gradient information as input. This model essentially acts as a reversed function of a standard Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN). We then investigate the possibility of training GHNNs from scratch by utilizing Hamiltonian Neural Stack Augmentation, an innovative method that leverages both augmented data and neural networks for improved performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of GHNNs through explicit gradient computations and showcase their applicability in sensitive settings such as private machine learning. Furthermore, we highlight the GHNN's potential to enhance the security of Hamiltonian Neural Networks in vulnerable positions within larger neural networks through the rectification of backdoors.

The consistency of AI models is paramount for their success in practical applications, yet they typically fall short of human expectations when first deployed. A significant issue is the absence of techniques to handle overconfidence in predictions, which can lead to substantial costs in terms of time, effort, and financial losses. Addressing this challenge becomes even more complicated when dealing with real-world applications, given the difficulty of rectifying trust issues through human-interventionist methods. Although retraining the model with human input is an option, it is hindered by the limited availability of high-quality data, which in turn hinders the improvement of the model. To tackle this cycle of low-confidence predictions, data shortages, and trust issues, we propose a framework that integrates multiple agents working together, where human trust ratings are used to prioritize predictions, and a separate agent focuses on enriching the dataset based on these ratings. When a prediction fails to meet human standards of trust, the model is retrained with the help of this enriched dataset, thereby breaking the cycle of trust issues, data shortages, and low-confidence predictions.

In recent years, X-ray-based baggage examination technology has gained popularity due to its high efficiency and reliability. However, sequence-based methods have been shown to be particularly vulnerable to sequence manipulation, which can compromise the security of such systems. To address this concern, a high-quality dataset called the X-ray Banned Items Dataset (XBID) has been created to facilitate research in this domain. The XBID dataset comprises a diverse range of forbidden items, along with detailed annotation guides to assist other researchers who wish to expand the dataset. To further enhance security, a novel Lateral Suppression Module (LSM) has been designed to prevent the manipulation of item sequences. The LSM module has been effectively integrated with existing sequence-based methods, resulting in improved performance and robustness against such attacks. The proposed XBID dataset and the LSM module have demonstrated superior results over previous security systems, showcasing a significant reduction in accuracy loss when faced with sequence manipulation attacks.

We've established a novel topological invariant, denoted by $Q_V$, that's linked to a specific type of object called a torus link chain. This invariant is based on the interaction of an object with a set of trivial torus knots, as defined by the averaged quantum 6j-symbols. Our analysis indicates that $Q_V$ can distinguish between different torus link chains, sharing a volume that exceeds the EMD of a single torus knot. Interestingly, $Q_V$ remains unchanged under various modifications to the object, including Dehn fillings and branchings. By comparing the values of $Q_V$, we can determine if two objects have isometric volumes. Furthermore, $Q_V$ exhibits behavior related to the Volume Hypothesis, as it is closely connected to the L^2 invariant and volume estimates. The relationship between $Q_V$ and other L^2 invariants, such as torsion volumes and Upsilon volumes, is explored, as is the connection between $Q_V$ and the superfluidity phase transition.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is to determine the contextually appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings.  Despite significant efforts, WSD remains an unsolved problem in NLP.  One promising approach to résolving this issue is through human crowd-sourcing, but it poses difficulties in scalability.  To address these challenges, we propose an unsupervised crowd-enforced framework called Context-gloss Enhancement for WSD.  This framework leverages a combination of human and automated sources to generate context and gloss combinations for each target word.  It utilizes a context-gloss pair representation based on both semantic and syntactic elements.  The inclusion of gloss information aids in capturing the part-of-speech (POS) of the target word, whereas the context context aids in capturing the sentence-level information.  To enhance the model's performance, we implement an iterative post-processing method that selects the most suitable context-gloss combination for each sentence.  We test our framework on the WordSenseLexical Database and achieve notable improvements over baseline systems, indicating its effectiveness in solving WSD problems.

A novel integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function has been developed, and it is shown that this formulation meets several desirable properties, including satisfaction of the boundary conditions, linearity, and preservation of the function's periodicity. A related paradox is also addressed, and it is demonstrated that the integral expression can be refined to eliminate the paradox. A hypothetical connection to the Dirac delta function in one dimension is also explored, along with an alternative regularization technique.

The paper discusses the strategy for detecting top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC, given the background suppression provided by heavy nucleus targets, which is equivalent to approximately 10 times the number of proton-proton collisions. With the CMS detector's capabilities, it is possible to identify top quarks with an efficiency of about 75% in events featuring two isolated muons and four jets originating from a single proton-nucleus interaction, which is equivalent to selecting one-in-five million proton-proton events. Furthermore, the paper examines the sensitivity of the CMS detector to the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus interactions at an 13 TeV energy level and discusses the statistical uncertainties associated with various cross-section measurements in proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions.

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL parsing, specifically column names, which are not addressed by existing works. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel column name prediction task as part of an end-to-end, cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing task. A key distinction between column name prediction and existing schema inference tasks is the reliance on only the input query instead of the underlying database table. To achieve high accuracy in column name prediction, we introduce three innovations: using a supportive task with partial annotations, designing a suitable neural input transformation, and introducing a column name prediction task as part of an end-to-end, cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing task with limited labels. The results of our supportive task show significant improvements in both accurate and natural-looking parsing metrics when compared to an baseline model. Moreover, our approach in natural-language processing and semantics achieves state-of-the-art results in the SuperGLUE Natural Language Inference, GLUE Natural Language Inference, SemEval-2017 Task 0, and TREC 2001 Natural Language Question Answering tasks.

Machine learning models reliant on sensitive data have gained popularity in recent years. However, ensuring the confidentiality of data during training has proven to be a challenging task. Researchers have explored various methods to encrypt data in a way that prevents the access of sensitive information, including gradient leakage. This paper surveys current techniques for differential confidentiality in graph-organized data, including novel applications and existing methods. We examine existing works through three categories: node classification based on partial graphs, comprehensive node classification, and network structure learning. Furthermore, we discuss open questions and consider future directions for this area of study.

As the large-scale astronomical missions like Euclid begin operation, its rate of image data and resulting scientific output will significantly surpass what can be achieved with human expertise alone. Thus, it is essential to invest in post-processing technologies that can automate and refine the analysis of Euclid data, enabling a broader range of researchers to explore its vast potential. In this context, we would like to present the Heritage Science Opportunities for the Euclid mission, which aims to provide a channel for researchers to engage with the extensive dataset made available by the mission. By leveraging Euclid's capabilities and resources, this initiative has the power to shape the field of cosmology and make notable contributions to the field of astronomy.

In this research, we propose an automatic method to generate challenging road networks for the evaluation of automated lane-keeping systems using B-spline curves and surfaces. To ensure safety, we create a system that prevents the generation of tight intersections and sharp curves, as they can pose risks to the system being tested. To assess the system's effectiveness, we develop an alternative method involving real-world data, and conduct statistical comparisons using a dataset of 2000 randomly generated road networks. Further, we examine the importance of controlling exit ramp curvature and the distance between adjacent roads, and find that our system meets the standards of leading industry leaders in this domain.

Captivating listeners with the essence of a music playlist has long been a challenge for music enthusiasts and professionals alike. To achieve this, one effective approach is to incorporate a descriptive element, much like the artwork found in album layouts. However, there is a significant obstacle to overcoming this challenge: the auditory nature of music. Since descriptors are typically written based on the actual sounds of the music, it raises the issue of what exactly the description would be conveying - the emotional impact of the music or its underlying melodic components? One innovative solution to this problem is Melody Captioning, an AI-powered technology that learns from vast musical databases and generates concise, yet insightful descriptions of a playlist's primary melodic themes. In turn, this technology has the potential to not only simplify music retrieval but also spark novel artistic ideas and even guide blind users in navigating their music libraries. Although MC is a complex task, our research demonstrates that by combining multiple learned features and employing a layering approach in our neural network, we can achieve remarkable results - our model accurately identifies 87.99% of melodic elements in a dataset consisting of 10 diverse genres.

A new method is presented that allows for the creation of a hydrodynamic model capable of predicting the random fluctuations of a quantum fluid in motion. Unlike traditional hydrodynamic approaches, this method does not rely on the assumption that hydrodynamics can be separated from quantum fluctuations. Instead, a set of correlated hydrodynamics and Bogoliubov quasi-particle modes is derived directly from a quantum Bose gas, with their respective contributions identifiable in different regimes of temperature and density. Various phenomena resulting from both interacting and non-interacting Bose gases are examined, with excellent agreement between the predicted values and those obtained through lattice simulations. The developed framework demonstrates its utility in investigating the interplay between quantum and thermal disorder, as well as the effects of quantum Regime Phase Transitions on Bose gases at low temperatures.

Temporal activity detection in videos is identified as a challenging task due to its broad range of possible occurrences. A key issue is the limited availability of annotated data, which can result in overfitting when using existing methods. This problem is further exacerbated by the limited range of annotated time segments within each video. To circumvent this difficulty, a new approach called DCAN has been proposed, which utilizes dual time context consolidation to reduce overfitting and learn context-aware temporal activity models. The proposed method uses two main context models: a segmentation-invariant context model and a segmentation-aware context model. The segmentation-invariant context model is utilized to learn video-level temporal activity patterns by consolidating unannotated time segments. In contrast, the segmentation-aware context model is employed to produce duration-aware time segments for each video. A dual time context consolidation network is then introduced, which integrates the two context models to a single network through a time segment generator. By selectively suppressing the time segment generator, the proposed method can switch between two operating modes: data-efficient learning of temporal activity models using unannotated time segments and training on annotated time segments using the time segment generator. The proposed DCAN achieves superior performance to existing state-of-the-art methods on ActivityNet v1.3 and TAST, with explicit evaluations of annotation efficiency and time segment generation.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic due to their complex formation processes. Research suggests that PTMs develop from an edge-localized instability, specifically an edge-chaos instability, as it causes magnetic fluctuations in the private region. These fluctuations then trigger an ELM-like filtration process, restricting the island's growth and contributing to its prolonged existence. PTMs have distinct characteristics, such as chaotic magnetic fields, isolated eddy patterns, and restricted access to the central plasma. The unique conditions within the private region allow for the temporary coexistence of intense plasma flows with counter-rotating directions. The observation of sharp magnetic gradient edges to PTMs suggests that these structures can influence plasma behavior near the X-point. The discovery of PTMs also highlights the importance of comprehensive edge diagnostics in tokamak plasmas.

This research focuses on preventing collisions among autonomous mobile robots moving autonomously in a two-dimensional space by utilizing Vector Field Methodology. It introduces an dynamic vortex potential field containing regions that can be updated dynamically to ensure the avoidance of static and dynamic obstacles. A variable reference frame approach is used to ensure that the target location is reached as efficiently as possible according to the new dynamic field. It also proves that the proposed methodology meets the requirements for a collaborative and learning robotic system. It further compares the performance of the proposed methodology to existing methods through simulation. It demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology in a real-world application by preventing collisions between a mobile robot and an autonomous aerial vehicle in its flight path. It also compares the performance of the proposed methodology to existing methods through simulation. It demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology in a real-world application by preventing collisions between a mobile robot and an autonomous aerial vehicle in its flight path.

As the quantity of available data grows, it's not uncommon for empirical frequency estimates to display an atypical behavior: around the mean, their standard deviation increases more slowly than anticipated, eventually surpassing the theoretical limit and indicating a bimodal distribution. In the case of Markov chain models, this phenomenon becomes more pronounced as the number of successive terms analyzed increases. In our research, we identify specific thresholds below which the standard deviation of frequency estimates follows the predicted square-root law; above these limits, the distribution becomes bimodal, and the standard deviation of estimated frequencies surpasses the law's limit by an ever-increasing amount, which is determined by the standard deviation of the largest eigenvalue of an associated stochastic matrix.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have been influenced by the potential of intelligent reflecting surfaces to optimize signal propagation. By adjusting their reflections, these surfaces can enhance various communication system performances. This study explores the application of intelligent reflecting surfaces in radar systems, specifically investigating how they can be integrated with radar technology to achieve better target parameter estimation. A numerical model is utilized to assess the radar's performance when the target is moving at different speeds and under different radar configurations. Furthermore, this study is complemented by a discussion on the optimization of radar frequency based on the target's reflection properties. However, it is observed that this approach is subject to the limitation that a unique frequency solution cannot be derived from the available mathematical expressions. Consequently, a novel formulation is proposed to overcome this challenge, yielding a strategy for optimizing the radar frequency.

Understanding the underlying technology of a fuzzer through static code analysis can be an effective method for creating more sophisticated testing tools. To regulate the level of complexity, researchers have established criteria such as context-dependent context-free grammar and Chomsky Normal Form to describe the desired scope of fuzzers. Although these standards facilitate comparison and exchange of knowledge among experts in this field, there is currently a lack of systematic comparison between various methods. To address this gap, we have conducted a comprehensive evaluation of different techniques used in the field, including context-dependent context-free grammar, Chomsky Normal Form, and context-free grammar with function calls. Our research demonstrates that no single approach stands out as significantly better than the others, thus indicating the need for a more flexible evaluation framework that considers the unique characteristics of each technique. To this end, we propose a new evaluation framework that assesses the generative capabilities of each method through the creation of a set of test cases. Our research also highlights the challenges associated with scaling up static analysis-based fuzzer evaluation, which could potentially be addressed by combining such methods with hybrid evaluation techniques.

Pretrained models have shown significant potential in ongoing learning tasks. However, the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark that examines their performance across various learning settings, which is crucial for further research. To address this gap, we introduce the Relearn Benchmark, a fundamental evaluation framework that investigates whether significant improvements can be achieved by pretrained models in tasks that have been previously learned. The Relearn Benchmark consists of three components, representing different levels of challenge: (1) refresher tasks, which assess learning retention after a prolonged period; (2) partial update tasks, which involve updating a pre-existing model with new data that includes some existing information; and (3) replacement tasks, which simulate the complete replacement of an existing model. Our research focuses on refresher and partial update tasks, using gluon-cifar10, a popular dataset. The results show that while pretrained models excel in refresher tasks, they may not always perform better in partial update tasks, potentially because the benefits of existing knowledge are offset by the risk of overfitting. The evaluation of the Relearn Benchmark is relevant to ongoing learning in continuous life scenarios and highlights the critical role of task difficulty and learning schedule in determining the outcomes.

We investigate minimal surfaces within a specific homotopy category in metric spaces, specifically focusing on surfaces that could be mapped to any given surface in a homotopy-friendly way, up to a category that includes homotopies. This study reveals that in certain metric spaces, including those derived from distances that are a combination of Euclidean distances, a surface will be part of the minimal surface category if it represents a unique starting point for homotopies. Additionally, we find that if a surface has a specific type of mapping to it, then that surface will be part of the minimal surface category. This research also shows that if a surface has a particular type of mapping to it, then that surface will be part of the minimal surface category.

This final installment of a three-part series builds on the previous research from parts I and II, which investigated the long-term behavior of the solution $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. Here, it is determined that if the initial condition $u_0$ is convergent, but not stable, then the solution $u$ is also unstable at infinity, and this instability is  robust for both smooth and nonsmooth data. Additionally, it is found that if the limit conditions are $u(-\infty, t) \to l$ and $u(\infty, t) \to m$, with $m \neq l$, then the solution $u$ will converge to a different limit $(m + l)/2$ as $x$ approaches either negative or positive infinity.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a null spin value have shown contrasting results when examining different two-body interactions across various configurations. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers suggest establishing a threshold for separation between excited and ground state configurations, and it appears that the 0+ ground state in 64Ni is uniquely positioned to meet this criterion due to its low energy level. A notable increase in the monopole strength component within the wave function makes up the theoretical framework used to explain this phenomenon. Furthermore, a thorough examination of this interaction's effect is conducted across a series of near-null spin states in 64Ni, and the results indicate that the monopole component plays a significant role in determining the configuration of these states. Consequently, a revised classification of the 0+ excited state in 64Ni is proposed, and it is predicted that a similar increase in the monopole component will be observed in the 0+ ground state of 62Ni, thus providing a basis for further experimental verification.

The theoretical foundations for analyzing complex general equilibrium situations relying on price mechanisms and nearly perfect competition among rational agents with access to full information has been well-laid by previous work based on the concepts of price mechanisms and competitive general equilibrium. To build upon this foundation, researchers need mechanisms that can efficiently determine equilibrium prices without prior knowledge of agents' preferences or their own actions, utilizing only limited inquiries into these preferences. The existing General Rational Equilibrium with Price Information (GREPI) framework requires the price mechanism to conduct an inquiry of a specific type into each agent's interdependent utility function to locate an equilibrium. Through the development of new information-theoretic approaches, this study introduces the concept of a utilitarian polytope sidecar to determine whether a specific utility function is nonnegative, achieving this by conducting only $2\log(1/\epsilon)^d$ inquiries into the utility function, provided $d$ represents the number of agents and $\epsilon$ represents the precision level. As a result, the study demonstrates that conducting $2d\log(3/(\epsilon\delta))$ inquiries into each agent's utility function is sufficient to find an equilibrium in games with Lipschitz payoffs, where $\delta$ represents the maximum Lipschitz constant among the payoffs.

When evaluating machine learning models using multiple folds of data, our research reveals that employing j-k fold cross-validation significantly reduces model variance when comparing nested models, thereby enabling more precise assessments of their differences. By conducting a theoretical and empirical analysis of this method, our study shows that utilizing j-k fold CV validates assumptions underlying the F-score and McNemar tests for nested models, whereas traditional k-fold CV leads to biased estimates of model variance. Our empirical results, spanning three NLP tasks and two k-fold iterations, demonstrate that j-k fold CV yields substantially lower variance when comparing nested models, a crucial consideration in critical applications such as clinical NLP, where confident comparisons between models are essential.

Over the years, student-instructor models have emerged as a top-performing approach in machine learning, particularly in tasks involving natural language processing. This paper delves into key aspects of these models from a functional standpoint, covering their design, execution, and ongoing development within the knowledge acquisition framework. As a cornerstone of artificial intelligence research, we examine embedding, attention mechanisms, and information flow – essential components that have been consistently utilized across various student-instructor configurations. As knowledge is continuously refined and updated, we investigate the role of iterative learning cycles, self-supervision, and meta-learning in both student-instructor models and the broader knowledge acquisition community. As real-world applications involving student-instructor models begin to emerge, we discuss their potential to shape the future of artificial intelligence in areas such as human-robot interaction, executive decision-making, and more.

We introduce a novel, efficient method for describing functions in graphical models, which we call Brief Function Depiction (BFD). By focusing on the most critical factors, BFD expedites the exact computation of MAP estimates and provides a useful proxy for purposes like data imputation and model evaluation. We demonstrate that utilizing BFD representations leads to significant enhancements in performance and a reduction in inference time for complex energy minimization problems in visual reconstruction applications. Specifically, our results indicate that BFD enables reliable and precise energy minimization in real-world scenes within a quarter of the time it would take for an exact approach. Furthermore, BFD enables significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency for applications like multi-view stereo and image segmentation.

We investigate how photon recoil affects the measurement of absorption cross-sections in a manner that's applicable to single-beam techniques. By considering an ultracold, overlapping light field of atoms, we show that a simple model can accurately account for the photon recoil using the 87Sr ground state. Due to the small moment of inertia of this system, we find that the absorption cross-section is remarkably insensitive to photon recoil, and thus it's feasible to recover precise absorption cross-sections even without accounting for this effect. Nonetheless, we find that in certain situations, particularly with larger optical dipole moments, the photon recoil can impede accurate recovery of the absorption cross-section. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the optimization of photon recoil correction methods for accurately determining absorption cross-sections.

The complex interplay between viscous fluid and flexible elastic structures gives rise to a diverse range of phenomena, from benign fluctuations to catastrophic failures. We study the interdependent evolution of fluid and elastic phases in cross-flow interactions by employing advanced microscopy to investigate the shear-induced transition in turbulent flow over a flexible flat plate. Our findings reveal a vast expansion of fluctuating modes beyond those predicted by linear theory and we identify an elevated parabolic region that signals the onset of significant elastic responses. This region is the critical locus of shear-induced transitions and we show that it is accurately defined by a simplified nonlinear model, without relying on linear theory. Our research provides a clear framework for analyzing the interaction between fluid and elastic structures and it is relevant to a broad range of applications involving fluid-elastic interactions.

The Racah algebra $R$ is a lesser-known extension of the Askey-Wilson algebra. It has multiple equivalent representations derived from the universal Askey-Wilson algebra $UAW$ by using isomorphisms that factor through the stabilizer $Z_n$ of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. In this paper, we analyze the structure of the stabilizer $Z_n$ and its relationship with the universal Askey-Wilson algebra $UAW$. Notably, $Z_n$ is an abelian extension of the Heisenberg algebra with central element $s$ and can be further divided into subalgebras based on $n$-division properties. We establish that $Z_n$ is responsible for generating the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the universal Askey-Wilson algebra $UAW$, and this series can be simplified using $n$-division polynomials. In addition, we can use the stabilizer $Z_n$ to obtain new representations of the Racah algebra $R$ by applying its isomorphism to the universal Askey-Wilson algebra $UAW$.

Our theory shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon modes may exhibit unusual behavior in the presence of a layer-imbalancing strain. This strain essentially separates the two layers by a minute displacement, causing a unique twist in the intralayer coupling. As a result, we found that the triplons could form a variety of unconventional states, including twisted superfluid and supersolid states, mediated by symmetry-breaking terms. These states require exact microscopic mechanisms to be stabilized and are distinguished by odd- parity amplitudes in the vacuum. We also found that the twisted superfluid state could be more stable than the conventional superfluid state, and that this state could be experimentally identified through measurements of magnetic susceptibility and sound mode softening. Additionally, we considered the applicability of our findings to biatomic honeycomb layer materials such as $^{17}$O-labeled Bi$_3$Pe$_2$ and predicted the twisted superfluid state could be identified experimentally using $^{17}$O NMR.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-nucleus collision events occurring when the WIMP and nucleus are at rest with respect to one another. We previously examined the mean speed of incident WIMPs required for a minimum recoil angle and the distribution of this speed in one dimensional cases. Building on that work, we are now calculating the probability distribution of recoil angles for a minimum collision energy in three dimensional scenarios, as well as the angular and energy spectra of final state WIMPs.

An online search engine's customization can result in the underestimation of publicly available information. We designed an experiment to verify this concept by observing user perception of a website with varying levels of relevant information displayed. The study was conducted in both lab and remote settings, with participants searching for information on a website tailored to their previous queries. Half of the participants saw a fully displayed website with extensive relevant information, while the other half viewed a partially hidden site with limited relevant info. Subsequent searches revealed that those who saw the partially hidden site had a harder time discovering all the available info, as evidenced by them missing roughly 40% of the relevant info when comparing it to those who saw the fully displayed site. This study demonstrates the potential risks of biased online results, especially in sensitive topics, and highlights the need for users to be aware of potential distortions in their online perception.

We are proposing the development of a cutting-edge muon-proton or muon-nucleus accelerator that operates at the TeV level, with the aim of advancing a diverse range of disciplines including particle astrophysics, particle physics, and nuclear physics. By doing so, we hope to gain a deeper understanding of how high-energy cosmic rays are produced, as well as the properties of rare particles such as long-lived kaons and heavy neutrinos that could provide valuable insights into the fundamental nature of matter. Furthermore, this accelerator has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of advanced detector technologies and the exploration of new avenues in physics beyond the Standard Model.

A novel approach is proposed to create high-quality, low-bandwidth 4D MRI datasets that can accommodate various breathing patterns, without the need for specific targeting of breathing cycles.
The method was inspired by the observation that lung regions serve as a reliable indicator for the entire body's respiratory movements.
Initially, a 3D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MRI protocol with elevated spatial resolution and reduced bandwidth is used to obtain imaging data that can be further processed to create a respiratory motion map.
Subsequently, a data-driven approach is employed to adjust the imaging data to account for distinct breathing phases, ultimately yielding a single 4D MRI dataset that can be obtained in about 5 minutes.
The proposed technique was compared to a conventional 4D MRI protocol in terms of respiratory motion coverage, image quality, and patient comfort, with the proposed method demonstrating comparable or superior performance in all aspects.

Recent research into Control Barrier Functions has shown great promise in creating secure and resilient control systems. However, the method's effectiveness is dependent on the availability of a suitable set of reference trajectories, which can be challenging to obtain, especially in dynamic scenarios. This paper explores the concept of Control Barrier Functions that are restricted by system input constraints, which could facilitate the development of more practical security solutions for complex systems affected by external disturbances. Additionally, we investigate the potential of using learning methods to automatically generate reference trajectories within predetermined boundaries, which could clad a system affected by external disturbances in a safety wrapper. This approach is theoretically valid for systems meeting specific criteria and is demonstrated with a tangible example involving a nonlinear mechanical system.

We introduce a novel approach to representing region shapes using CF-approximation areas, a flexible and scalable framework that encompasses and expands upon existing methods such as level sets, boundary representations, and binary images to facilitate tasks like collision detection, motion planning, and volume calculation. This model's versatility is showcased through its ability to smoothly map between different representations of a region's shape as its bounding surface or volume changes. To efficiently handle regions with complex boundaries, we propose a suite of CF-approximation area-based algorithms that prioritize balance, efficiency, and simplicity, leveraging CF-approximations that can be computed directly from level set fields, and automatically adjust to accommodate changes in a region's surface or volume, offering substantial performance improvements over legacy methods like boundary representations and signed distance functions, especially when dealing with large numbers of objects in higher dimensional spaces.

To enhance the effectiveness of progressive testing in complex software systems, reliable risk-based testing metrics are crucial. Although the Paired-Permutation Importance Paired with Coverage (PPIPC) technique has been suggested for assessing the importance of software components, there is a lack of clear PPPIC guidelines suitable for real-world applications. To address this issue, a new set of guidelines called Precise Paired-Permutation Examination for Structured Test Metrics (PPES) has been proposed to facilitate the design of reliable and efficient progression testing strategies. The PPES framework is designed to be adaptable to various system structures and can be used to create structured test cases that are more efficient and cost-effective, as demonstrated through a case study involving a real-world software application. The study shows that the PPES framework can produce a more reasonable cost-effectiveness index and a more efficient testing path compared to the original PPPIC technique. The findings from this research can be used to guide practitioners in designing reliable and efficient progression testing strategies for complex software systems.

This research provides a comprehensive public dataset consisting of historical and
current information on freight costs and shipping volume from 1966 to 2022 for six
major cargo types, including tankers, containers, and other vessel types. Until now,
there has been a lack of accessible and unified data on these topics, hampering
research and analysis in the academic field. By assembling and combining data from
reliable sources such as the Marine Transportation Costs database, Top Shipping
Database, and Historical Annals of Shipping, we have created a comprehensive
dataset available for public use, featuring the daily price of freight, monthly
shipping volumes, new vessel constructions, purchased vessels, and scrapped vessels
for each cargo type. To facilitate exploration and discovery, we have included
summary statistics on the structure of global shipping volumes, freight cost, new
vessel constructions, purchased vessels, and scrapped vessels. We have also
determined the cross-sectional correlation between shipping volumes and freight costs,
finding no significant historical linear relationship between these two variables
over the past fifty-seven years. Additionally, we have identified the top twenty
correlated variables with the mean freight cost and shipping volume among all cargo
types. Furthermore, we have the opportunity to study other variables influencing
freight cost and shipping volume, such as global economic indicators, oil prices,
containerization, and the 2008 financial crisis. We invite researchers across
